headline: High-risk shared filesystem/MCP pair: prompt injection, data leakage, and write conflicts are plausible by default; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents use MCP and can ingest files; Agent A explicitly shares state via filesystem and git, while Agent B processes PDFs/text/images and uses MCP. That creates a plausible instruction-injection bridge through shared content, even though no direct parser weakness is documented. Uncertainty does not lower severity because the pathway exists in default workflows.
conditions: IF Agent A writes attacker-controlled text into a shared repo or file that Agent B later reads as guidance
IF Agent B ingests a document containing embedded instructions and forwards them into MCP-driven actions
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Disable MCP on one side for untrusted content
Add a manual review step before Agent B acts on file-derived instructions
Use a read-only mount for shared inputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for file-originated instructions

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A reads and writes filesystem content and handles shell environment data; Agent B processes documents and images and sends requests to multiple third-party model APIs by default. If they share a workspace, sensitive files touched by A can flow into B's uploads or prompts. The pairwise leakage path is credible from the profiles alone, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same directory or document set
IF Agent B uploads file contents from that shared workspace to a remote model API
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent
Remove secrets from shared files before either agent runs
Restrict Agent B to local-only models for sensitive inputs
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent A can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; Agent B also supports MCP and broad network egress, so both can mutate shared resources if pointed at the same workspace. The profiles explicitly say A shares state via filesystem and git, which makes concurrent write conflicts and repository corruption likely in default multi-instance use. Uncertainty favors the higher severity.
conditions: IF both agents are run against the same git repository or output directory
IF Agent B writes generated diagrams or files while Agent A edits the same paths
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories
Serialize writes with a lock file
Pause one agent during commits or exports
Use separate git branches per agent
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can generate or edit code and files, and Agent B is a document-processing agent that can turn inputs into diagrams or other outputs. If B treats A's outputs as authoritative, errors can cascade from code or text into downstream artifacts. The profiles do not prove blind trust, so medium fits the inferred default workflow.
conditions: IF Agent B consumes Agent A's generated text or files without verification
IF Agent A's incorrect output is used as source material for a diagram or document
mitigations: Require human review before B renders or publishes A's output
Add a verification checklist for extracted facts
Keep source and derived artifacts in separate folders
Mark A-generated content as untrusted in filenames
requires-engineering: add automated consistency checks

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A handles shell environment data and optional Google account login/API keys; Agent B handles API keys and can call multiple external model providers. The profiles show broad remote processing but no residency or retention guarantees, so compliance mismatch is plausible for regulated data. I do not cite only one agent because the risk arises from the pair's combined external exposure.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either agent's prompts or files
IF the deployment requires residency, retention, or processor controls not documented in the profiles
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both tools
Use only approved local or region-compliant backends
Review vendor DPAs and retention settings before use
Disable optional account login where unnecessary
requires-engineering: implement policy-based routing by data class
